clue.text: Cleaner state required for this rag

blocks.note: a daily is a British name for a woman who comes in to clean a house
to state something is to put it into words

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady announces what you need to know about a scruffy newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Express is a British tabloid; Private Eye habitually calls newspapers rags.
explanation.definitionFit: Rag is a dismissive slang word for a newspaper, and this British tabloid is a fine example of one.

clue.text: One broadcast additional affair

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard rather than read, so we want a spelling of a word that is spoken

blocks.note: one is the indefinite article a
additional means more, and the ending of the French word is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: A news item reveals that someone has been having an extra affair.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for love is used in English for a love affair, often an illicit one.

clue.text: Not a busy period, as one's silly moo comes first

indicators.note: silly suggests nonsense, so these letters are jumbled into a sensible order
tells us the cow's noise is placed at the front rather than after the other part

blocks.note: to low is to make the sound of cattle
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone explains a quiet time as being down to a foolish cow putting itself at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The off-peak part of the year, when hotels and resorts have few visitors, is quiet and cheap.

clue.text: Miliband having to pull up before victory? His reign was brief

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
places the leader's name and the pulled word ahead of the victory sign

blocks.note: Ed Miliband, Labour leader until 2015
to draw is to pull, as a cart is drawn
V for victory

explanation.surface: Ed Miliband must retreat before he can win, and his time in charge was short.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward V was one of the Princes in the Tower; he reigned for about two months in 1483 and was never crowned.
explanation.definitionFit: This English king held the throne for only a few weeks before being deposed and vanishing.

clue.text: Photograph 'leg man' showing self-control

indicators.note: showing means putting on display, so the answer is on view inside these words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the second into the start of the third

explanation.surface: A picture of a man who admires legs reveals his composure.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'leg man' look like the subject, but it simply carries the answer across its word breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides mucus, the word means calm composure, from the old humour thought to make people stolid.

clue.text: One forced to leave seductress when penetrated by a stick

indicators.note: something penetrated has another thing pushed inside it

blocks.note: Eve tempted Adam with the apple in Genesis
taken as written
a cue is the stick used in snooker and billiards

explanation.surface: A temptress is driven out after being run through with a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone moved out of a dangerous area, such as a child sent from a city in wartime, has been made to leave home.

clue.text: Frosty Lib-Dems harbouring old writers

indicators.note: a harbour holds ships inside it, so the words here hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words; the rest is cover

explanation.surface: Chilly Liberal Democrats are sheltering some aged authors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writers' suggests people, but here they are the pointed tools used to write.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylus was the pointed instrument ancient Romans used to scratch letters into wax tablets.

clue.text: Brenda-like state – joke getting in charge

blocks.note: MA is the abbreviation for Massachusetts, a US state
a jest is a joke
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: Royal pomp turns into a laughing matter when a joker is put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: Being like the Queen means having regal dignity, the grandeur of Her Majesty herself.

clue.text: Conference pressure that hurt Western and Other World leaders

indicators.note: leaders are at the front, so only the opening letter of each word counts

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
the cry of someone saying that hurt
W is the abbreviation for Western
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A summit puts painful strain on the leaders of the West and the rest of the world.
explanation.definitionFit: A pow-wow, originally a Native American council, is used informally for any meeting or discussion.

clue.text: Skip Corby's ultimate corny bit for 2016?

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the final letter of the name is used

blocks.note: to skip is to jump or leap
the final letter of the name
an ear is the part of a corn plant holding the grain

explanation.surface: Jeremy Corbyn ends up skipping a corny line of the current year's speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Corby is Private Eye's shortening of Jeremy Corbyn. The question mark shows 2016 is an example: it had a 29 February.
explanation.definitionFit: Any year with an extra day in February, such as 2016, is one of these.

clue.text: Jumpy little thing's regret of getting tossed

indicators.note: things that are tossed are thrown about and land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A nervous child's remorse at being thrown around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpy' looks like nervousness, but it is literal: the creature leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A small amphibian living in trees that jumps from branch to branch is a hopping little creature.

clue.text: (& 21dn.) Side with utter sexist leader, Trump's country

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

blocks.note: United is the name of many football sides, such as Manchester United
to utter is to state
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Backing a crude chauvinist leader is what Trump's nation does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side with' reads as a verb meaning support, but 'Side' is a team and 'with' simply joins it on.
explanation.definitionFit: Donald Trump was elected US President in November 2016, so the nation became his to lead.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) What Charles has to stand for, though not necessarily sharing its sentiment?

definitions.text: What Charles has to stand for, though not necessarily sharing its sentiment?

blocks.clueFragment: What Charles has to stand for
blocks.note: surface reading: the principles the Prince of Wales must represent

blocks.clueFragment: though not necessarily sharing its sentiment
blocks.note: setter's reading: the tune he must rise to his feet for, whose wish for his mother's long life he may privately not share as he waits to be king

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand for' means represent, but also literally stand up when a tune is played; Charles was heir to his mother for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: The British national anthem prays for a long reign for the monarch, and everyone stands when it is played.

clue.text: Drug-taking Russian athlete, maybe, of most unusual proportions

blocks.note: first meaning: a competitor at the Games, a reference to the Russian doping scandal
second meaning: godlike, immense, like the gods of Mount Olympus

explanation.walkthrough: Russia's athletes were banned from the 2016 Rio track events over state-sponsored doping.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a competitor at the Games, and as an adjective means lofty and superhuman in scale.

clue.text: A good chance to score with screwing a-plenty

indicators.note: screwing twists things round, so these letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lad's boast that plenty of sex makes for a good chance of scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a spot kick from twelve yards is very likely to produce a goal.

clue.text: One given a bed for the night, calling "It's a fix!"

blocks.note: one is the indefinite article a

blocks.clueFragment: given a bed for the night
blocks.note: to put someone up is to let them stay overnight
a calling is a vocation or job

explanation.surface: An overnight guest cries foul, claiming the result was rigged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rigged in advance to deceive, with the outcome arranged beforehand, is a fraud or swindle.

clue.text: How the race was won? Corby, down to last 40% and a sheer audacity

indicators.note: reduced to the final two-fifths of a five-letter name, so only its closing pair is kept

blocks.note: the last two of the five letters
taken as written
neck is British slang for cheek or nerve

explanation.surface: Corbyn's leadership contest was won by cutting his rival down and sheer brass nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Corby is Private Eye's name for Jeremy Corbyn.
explanation.definitionFit: In horse racing a winner by the length of a horse's neck has won by a narrow margin.

clue.text: Virgin possibly set to follow ex-cabinet minister

indicators.note: the television set comes after the politician, so it goes at the end

blocks.note: Vince Cable was Business Secretary in the coalition government until 2015
a set is a television

explanation.surface: A former minister lines up behind a virgin, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Virgin Media is a UK cable television and broadband company.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgin Media supplies television down underground lines to British homes, an example of the service.

clue.text: Taking China's lead, churns out champ

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is taken
out suggests something put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of the country's name
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Following China's example, a country produces a champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champ' looks like a winner, but here it is the verb meaning to chew noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: To champ is to munch or crunch with the jaws, and this word means the same noisy crushing.

clue.text: Choir managed to take drugs for so long

indicators.note: something managed has been handled and arranged, so the letters are reorganised

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
E is ecstasy, so two of them are drugs

explanation.surface: A choir has been on drugs for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual British ways of saying goodbye to someone as they leave.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Cameron hiding survey dividing top social classes – that's cool

indicators.note: something hiding another thing keeps it inside, out of sight
a thing dividing a pair sits between them, splitting them apart

blocks.note: A and B are the top two grades in the UK's social classification
David Cameron was Prime Minister until 2016
lo means look, as in lo and behold

explanation.surface: David Cameron keeps a poll quiet as it splits the upper classes, and acts unruffled about it.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two containers: the survey goes inside the Prime Minister, and that whole unit then sits between the two class letters. Social grades A, B, C1 and so on are a British market-research scale.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping your cool means staying calm, and this word is self-assured composure under pressure.

clue.text: Where, abroad, Heath's gay proclivity exposed?

blocks.note: the French for where
Ted Heath, Conservative Prime Minister 1970 to 1974

explanation.surface: Asking where overseas Edward Heath's rumoured homosexuality was revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2015 police publicly investigated claims about the late Ted Heath's private life.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose homosexuality is made public without consent has been revealed against their will.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Seconds taken off bonking etc with endless battery component application

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for seconds

clue.text: Whisky-covered, tear-spilling bully

indicators.note: spilt things scatter and lose their order
something covered has another thing wrapped round it

blocks.note: malt is single malt whisky
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A drunk, weeping thug spilling whisky over himself.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully someone is to treat them cruelly and abuse them, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Rebuff from upset Brenda: "In Paris one gets caught short"

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina
je is French for I, the first person
CT is a shortened form of caught

explanation.surface: The Queen, in a huff, recalls a French outing where she was caught short and needed a loo.
explanation.walkthrough: Being caught short is British slang for urgently needing a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuff an offer or person is to turn it down or refuse it.

clue.text: Which gives warning before Labour MPs probably go their separate ways?

definitions.text: Which gives warning before Labour MPs probably go their separate ways?

blocks.clueFragment: Labour MPs probably go their separate ways
blocks.note: surface reading: the Labour Party splitting apart, as seemed likely in 2016
setter's reading: the alarm in Parliament that rings before MPs vote by walking into separate lobbies

explanation.walkthrough: In the Commons a vote is a division: members split into Aye and No lobbies, summoned by a ringing alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: Westminster's alert rings for eight minutes to summon MPs to vote in a division.
